subject: Anthropology
title: Social Stratification
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Social Stratification.

hook.text: One grave holds gold jewelry and fine pottery. The next holds nothing but bones. Inequality is written in burials.

buildup.text: Social stratification is the division of society into ranked layers based on wealth, power, and prestige.

discovery.text: Archaeology detects stratification through burial goods, house sizes, diet differences, and access to luxury items.

twist.text: Stratification wasn't inevitable. It emerged with surplus. When there's more than enough, someone always takes more.

climax.text: Material inequality leaves material traces. Archaeology reads social hierarchy directly from the ground.

punchline.text: Graves reveal who had power and who didn't.

quiz.question: How do archaeologists detect social stratification?
options: Through burial goods, house sizes, and diet differences
By asking descendants of ancient people

details.summary: Archaeological evidence for social stratification includes differences in burial treatment, house size, diet quality, and access to prestige goods. Inequality appears to have increased dramatically with agriculture, urbanization, and the formation of states.
details.whyItMatters: Archaeology can trace when and how human societies became unequal. This matters because inequality is often presented as natural and inevitable, but the archaeological record shows that egalitarian living was humanity's norm for most of history.
takeaways: Burial differences, house sizes, and diets reveal past inequality
Inequality increased dramatically with agriculture and states
Egalitarian societies were the norm for most of human history

faq.question: How do archaeologists detect social inequality without written records?
faq.answer: Rich versus poor burials, large versus small houses, differences in nutritional health from skeletal analysis, and unequal access to exotic trade goods all indicate stratification. Labor investment in monumental buildings implies organized inequality and coerced labor.

faq.question: When did social inequality first appear?
faq.answer: Hints of status differences appear among some complex hunter-gatherer societies, but marked inequality expanded with agriculture starting around 10,000 years ago. The rise of states around 5,000 years ago dramatically intensified stratification into rigid class systems.
